findings.headline: Capital Projects Financing Reserve of £9.3m provides thin cover against refinancing cost shock
findings.detail: The council has earmarked £9.3m in the Capital Projects Financing Reserve to mitigate adverse interest rate and investment return fluctuations, and specifically to fund additional borrowing costs from PWLB rates higher than assumed in project business cases. The difference between current PWLB rates (6.30%) and budgeted rates creates an annual cost gap that would consume the reserve within ~4.8 years.
findings.matters: The reserve is modest relative to the £57.96m internal borrowing that will eventually require external refinancing. If capital acceleration occurs or rates rise further, the reserve could deplete quickly, leaving no buffer for cost overruns or additional rate rises.
findings.figures: Capital Projects Financing Reserve £9,296,075. Implied annual refinancing cost gap at current rates ~£1.95m (£3,820,756 potential future interest less £1,865,950 budgeted).
findings.quote: The Council has an earmarked revenue reserve to mitigate against possible adverse fluctuations in the returns received from the council's investments and external borrowing costs, called the Capital Projects Financing Reserve. The balance in this reserve as at 31 March 2026 was £9,296,075.

findings.headline: Internal borrowing £57.96m and rising; refinancing to external at 6.30% would add £1.95m annual interest cost
findings.detail: West Suffolk's internal borrowing increased by £8.27m to £57.96m during 2025-26, while external borrowing fell from £9.25m to £9m. The council is funding its capital requirement from cash reserves (now £27.8m, above the £20m forecast) rather than external borrowing. Converting all internal borrowing to 40-year PWLB Certainty Rate borrowing at 6.30% would incur annual interest of £3.82m, versus the budgeted £1.87m—an annual gap of £1.95m.
findings.matters: Internal borrowing relies on available cash; once capital projects spend down reserves, external refinancing becomes mandatory. The rate jump from 1.84% existing to 6.30% new creates a cliff of unexpected additional borrowing costs. This affects debt affordability and could pressure the revenue budget once capital is deployed.
findings.figures: Internal borrowing £57,963,592 (up from £49,688,598). Cash held £27,810,000 vs forecast £20,000,000. At 6.30% PWLB Certainty Rate, annual interest on internal borrowing would be £3,820,756 vs budgeted £1,865,950.
findings.quote: if we were to transfer all of that internal borrowing to a 40 year PWLB loan using the 6.30 percent Certainty Rate, the Council would incur an initial annual interest payable cost of £3,820,756 (including our current external borrowing). This compares to our interest payable budget for 2025 to 2026 of £1,865,950.

findings.headline: Capital programme £44.9m underspent, with borrowing requirement only 60% of budget
findings.detail: The council budgeted a £111.9m borrowing requirement to fund capital projects in 2025-26, but actual borrowing requirement at year-end was £66.96m—a £44.9m shortfall (40%). This reflects delayed capital expenditure across major projects including Mildenhall Hub, West Suffolk Operational Hub, Bury Leisure Centre Improvement, and the Net Zero Community Energy Plan. The council's Capital Financing Requirement increased by £8.02m, but was entirely absorbed by internal borrowing from cash reserves rather than external borrowing.
findings.matters: Capital programme delays create delivery risk on strategic projects and defer revenue cost recognition. More importantly, when projects accelerate and cash depletes, the council will need to externally borrow at PWLB Certainty Rates now at 6.30% for 40-year terms—342 basis points above the 1.84% rate on existing debt.
findings.figures: Budgeted capital borrowing requirement £111,859,015; actual £66,963,592 (variance £44,895,423, 40% underspent).
findings.quote: Borrowing costs only form part of the Councils revenue budget once the project has been completed, so although there may be a borrowing requirement, until such time as the project is complete there will be no MRP or interest payable as part of the revenue budget.

findings.headline: The council is funding the reserve from a one-off Business Rates Equalisation contribution, having previously relied on New Homes Bonus grants which no longer appear available
findings.detail: The only reserve contribution in the forecast period is £2.5m from the Business Rates Equalisation Reserve in 2026/27. The document explicitly states 'The primary source for the funding of this reserve has previously been the New Homes Bonus Grant', indicating a material loss of a previous funding stream. No further contributions of any kind are planned in 2027/28, 2028/29, or 2029/30.
findings.matters: The loss of New Homes Bonus as a source and reliance on a one-off Business Rates contribution signals declining certainty of reserve replenishment. This reinforces that the depletion will be permanent and the council's forward capital funding will depend on borrowing capacity or revenue savings.
findings.figures: Business Rates Equalisation contribution £2,500,000 in 2026/27; zero contributions in all subsequent years
findings.quote: Contribution from the Business Rates Equalisation Reserve 2,500,000 0 0 0... The primary source for the funding of this reserve has previously been the New Homes Bonus Grant.

findings.headline: Four major capital projects account for £6.9m of the £7.8m reserve deployment: leisure investment (£3.2m combined), business incubation (£2m), and Haverhill regeneration (£727k)
findings.detail: The largest single withdrawal is the Leisure Investment Fund at £2.5m, supplemented by a Leisure Net Zero Investment Fund (£700k) and St Felix leisure provision (£752,608). These leisure funds alone represent £3.95m. The Business Park Incubation Centre will draw £2m. Haverhill High Street Fund takes £727,189 and is 'part funded from Growth Area Initiative monies'. These are discretionary capital investments, not forced operational spending.
findings.matters: Large discretionary capital investments funded from reserves signal the council's growth and regeneration priorities, and indicate it is willing to deplete financial buffers to pursue these objectives. Once reserves are spent, future capital will require borrowing or revenue reduction.
findings.figures: Leisure Investment Fund £2,500,000; Leisure Net Zero Investment Fund £700,000; St Felix leisure £752,608; Business Park Incubation £2,000,000; Haverhill High Street Fund £727,189
findings.quote: Capital Programme Leisure Investment Fund (2,500,000)... Capital Programme Leisure Net Zero Investment Fund (700,000)... Capital Programme St Felix, Newmarket, Leisure Provision (752,608)... Capital Programme Suffolk Business Park - Incubation Centre (AME) (2,000,000)... Haverhill High Street Fund... (727,189)

findings.headline: Revenue Support Grant is declining by £1.368m (17%) over three years, creating structural budget pressure.
findings.detail: Government grant funding (Revenue Support Grant) falls from £8,220 thousands in 2026-27 to £6,852 thousands in 2028-29, a reduction of £1,368k. The Adjustment Support Grant also phases out entirely by 2029-30. This structural loss of funding is being offset by council tax increases rather than spending reductions.
findings.matters: Declining government funding reduces the proportion of council spending covered by the government, increasing reliance on local taxation and debt, and may indicate a worsening spending/funding gap that cannot be closed by efficiency alone.
findings.figures: Revenue Support Grant: £8,220k (2026-27), £6,852k (2028-29); Adjustment Support Grant: £1,173k (2026-27) to £0 (2029-30)

findings.headline: Interest on borrowing increases 27.6% in year 2, from £2.334m to £2.977m, signalling rising debt burden.
findings.detail: The council's interest on borrowing rises sharply from £2,334 thousands in 2026-27 to £2,977 thousands in 2027-28. This is accompanied by increases in Minimum Revenue Provision (debt repayment) from £1,694 thousands to £2,292 thousands in the same period, indicating the council is borrowing significantly.
findings.matters: Rapidly rising borrowing costs reduce headroom in the revenue budget and are a signal of either planned capital borrowing or refinancing at worse rates; lenders need to understand the source and purpose of this debt.
findings.figures: Interest on borrowing: £2,334k (2026-27), £2,977k (2027-28); Minimum Revenue Provision: £1,694k (2026-27), £2,292k (2027-28)
findings.quote: Interest on borrowing 4 2,334 2,977 2,892 2,811

findings.headline: Earmarked reserves are being drawn down rapidly, declining from £47.5m to £30.4m over the five-year period.
findings.detail: In the first year alone, the council withdraws £12.732m from earmarked reserves (nearly 27% of the opening balance). Subsequent years see smaller but persistent draws of £1.4-1.5m annually. By 31 March 2030-31, reserves will have declined by £17.1m, reducing the council's financial buffer.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion limits the council's ability to absorb unexpected costs or revenue shortfalls, and may indicate unsustainable spending or use of one-off funding sources rather than sustainable revenue.
findings.figures: Opening earmarked reserves £47,454k, closing balance 2030-31 £30,361k; first year contribution (from reserves) (12,732)
findings.quote: Contributions to / (from) reserves 33 (12,732) (1,537) (1,414) (1,410)

findings.headline: Budget projections show deficits of £1.243m and £3.181m in years 3 and 4 with no identified funding solution.
findings.detail: The council is projecting balanced budgets for 2026-27 and 2027-28, but the medium-term financial strategy shows 'Remaining budget gap' of (1,243) thousands of pounds in 2028-29 and (3,181) thousands of pounds in 2029-30. The document does not show how these deficits will be funded or what savings will bridge the gap.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand whether the council has a credible plan to balance its budget and whether deficits will be covered by reserves or further borrowing.
findings.quote: Remaining budget gap 9 0 0 (1,243) (3,181)

findings.headline: Minimum Revenue Provision rising from £1,220k to £2,436k over four years, more than doubling
findings.detail: MRP is forecast to increase from £1,220k in 2025-26 to £1,767k in 2026-27, then £2,357k in 2027-28, and £2,436k in 2028-29. MRP reflects the debt repayment portion of the revenue budget required to cover past and current capital expenditure. This rising profile shows the council will be tied into substantial multi-year debt servicing commitments.
findings.matters: Rising MRP represents an increasing commitment of annual revenue budget to debt repayment, reducing flexibility for service spending. Combined with the rising financing costs indicator, this shows the council faces multi-year pressure on revenue resources.

findings.headline: £56.34m of capital expenditure underspends carried forward from 2025-26 capital budget
findings.detail: The document notes that the stated capital expenditure figures do not include potential capital carry-forward from underspends in the 2025-26 capital budget, currently forecast at £56.34m. This substantial amount is contingent on the S151 Officer's decisions about funding sources and could materially increase future capital programmes and borrowing requirements.
findings.matters: Large underspends indicate capital delivery challenges or over-programming. When these underspends are spent, they will increase the capital financing requirement and borrowing costs beyond the figures in this plan, amplifying the affordability pressures already flagged by the financing costs spike.
findings.quote: These figures do not include any potential capital expenditure carried forward from underspends in the 2025 to 2026 capital budgets, currently forecast to be £56.34 million.

findings.headline: Council plans to borrow £19.85m in 2026-27 for capital expenditure, with no planned borrowing in the following three years
findings.detail: The capital expenditure financing table shows £19.85m of borrowing funding the 2026-27 capital programme (out of total gross capital expenditure of £40.55m), with nil borrowing in 2027-28 through 2029-30. The concentration of borrowing into a single year drives the spike in financing costs indicators.
findings.matters: The front-loaded borrowing creates multi-year revenue implications through debt servicing costs. A lender would want to understand what capital schemes are driving this £19.85m borrowing and whether the council can sustain the resulting financing costs.

findings.headline: Financing costs as a proportion of revenue budget forecast to jump from 4.63% to 15.06% in 2026-27, more than tripling
findings.detail: West Suffolk's prudential indicator for financing costs to net revenue stream shows the proportion of the revenue budget committed to borrowing costs more than tripling from 4.63% forecast in 2025-26 to 15.06% in 2026-27, and continuing to rise to 18.88% in 2027-28. This signals either significantly increased borrowing or material revenue reduction, creating substantial pressure on available resources for service delivery.
findings.matters: Lenders need to understand the drivers of a three-fold increase in financing costs relative to revenue, and whether the council's borrowing strategy creates unsustainable pressures. For finance directors, this represents a major commitment of revenue budget to debt servicing at a time when councils face spending pressures.

findings.headline: Housing options reserve grows from £2.1m to £3.5m despite overall reserve decline
findings.detail: While total reserves shrink, the housing options reserve is built up deliberately over the plan period. It grows from £2.1m to £3.5m through net contributions averaging £350k per year, with contributions of £1.4–1.6m offset by withdrawals of £1.0–1.3m annually.
findings.matters: Against a backdrop of declining reserves, growth in housing response funding indicates council prioritization of housing pressures. This signals either expected housing demand or a commitment to housing investment, which a lender should understand as a strategic choice.

findings.headline: Total budgeted reserves fall from £47.5m to £30.4m — a 36% decline over four years
findings.detail: Combined reserves drop by £12.7m (27%) in year one alone, from £47.5m to £34.7m, then continue declining to £30.4m by 2029-2030. This represents sustained reserve drawdown with only modest contributions offsetting much larger withdrawals.
findings.matters: Declining reserves over a multi-year period signal structural imbalance between spending and income. Councils unable to maintain or grow reserves over time face reduced financial resilience and may face future constraints on borrowing or service delivery.

findings.headline: Building repairs reserve for leisure facilities depleted to zero by end of 2026-2027 and remains zero throughout the plan
findings.detail: The leisure building repairs reserve of £232k is drawn down completely in year one, with withdrawals (£532k) exceeding opening balance and contributions (£300k). Once empty, annual £300k contributions are matched by equivalent withdrawals, keeping the reserve at zero through 2029-2030.
findings.matters: A zero reserve for leisure building maintenance indicates either completion of works or inability to accumulate buffers for future repairs, reducing the council's flexibility to handle emergency maintenance or asset preservation.
findings.figures: Opening £232,438; 2026-27 withdrawal (£532,438); closing £0 thereafter

findings.headline: Strategic MTFS reserve drawn down by £7.8m in year one, leaving only £415k buffer
findings.detail: The council's main strategic contingency reserve opens at £5.7m but is withdrawn by £7.8m in 2026-2027, with only a £2.5m transfer offsetting the drawdown. The closing balance falls to £415k. This is the thinnest buffer in the four-year plan.
findings.matters: The MTFS reserve is a council's primary contingency for unexpected events or budget pressures. Heavy drawdown in year one of the plan signals the 2026-2027 budget is under strain and depends on using accumulated reserves.
findings.figures: Opening £5,704,235; withdrawal (£7,788,269); closing £415,966; transfer in £2,500,000
findings.quote: Strategic priorities and Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) reserve - see also appendix 3a 5,704,235 0 (7,788,269) 2,500,000 415,966

findings.headline: Property income revised downward by £0.27m in 2026/27 due to void allowances, particularly office units
findings.detail: Council is making increased provision for void/unlet properties across the portfolio, with particular pressure on office units. Creates £0.27m adverse variance in 2026/27, easing to £0.02m benefit in later years.
findings.matters: Commercial property market weakness is affecting council's asset base; office sector weakness is material
findings.figures: £0.27m pressure in 2026/27
findings.quote: Property income revisions, based on occupancy rates and projected rent reviews. Includes an allowance for potential void properties - particularly office units 0.27 (0.02) (0.02) (0.02)

findings.headline: West Suffolk House income loss of £0.16m from partner tenant vacancy in 2026/27
findings.detail: A commercial tenant is vacating from council-owned property, reducing income by £0.16m in 2026/27, stepping down to £0.10m in 2027/28, then ceasing. Council notes it is 'looking to mitigate impact in the medium to longer term' but provides no detail on mitigation.
findings.matters: Shows real estate portfolio vulnerability and loss of diversity in income streams; mitigation strategy is unspecified
findings.quote: Reduced income at West Suffolk House, as a result of a partner vacating the premises, looking to mitigate impact in the medium to longer term 0.16 0.10 0.00 0.00

findings.headline: Adjustment Support Grant is unconfirmed from 2027/28, creating uncertainty over £1.08m-£1.17m funding
findings.detail: Council assumes £1.17m of Adjustment Support Grant in 2026/27 but explicitly notes it is 'unconfirmed from 2027 to 2028'. The grant is assumed to continue at £1.08m (2027/28) and £1.02m (2028/29) but falls to zero in 2029/30.
findings.matters: Central government grant funding is uncertain beyond 2026/27, adding material risk to the medium-term financial plan
findings.figures: £1.17m (2026/27); unconfirmed 2027/28 onwards
findings.quote: Adjustment Support Grant (unconfirmed from 2027 to 2028) (1.17) (1.08) (1.02) 0.00

findings.headline: Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) payments create new annual cost of £1.77m across the MTFS
findings.detail: A mandatory environmental regulation cost of £1.77m recurring annually from 2026/27 through 2029/30. This appears to be a structural new burden rather than a one-off.
findings.matters: A significant new cost that cannot be avoided and reduces financial headroom; without this cost, the budget position would be materially stronger
findings.figures: £1.77m per year
findings.quote: Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) Payments (1.77) (1.77) (1.77) (1.77)

findings.headline: Revenue Support Grant declining 16.8% from £8.22m to £6.85m across the MTFS
findings.detail: Government funding is contracting systematically: from £8.22m in 2026/27 to £7.56m in 2027/28 and £6.85m in 2028/29, where it stabilizes. This is a structural loss of revenue.
findings.matters: Core government funding is shrinking, reducing the council's financial flexibility and contributing directly to the budget gaps that emerge later
findings.quote: Revenue Support Grant (8.22) (7.56) (6.85) (6.85)

findings.headline: Budget gap emerges in outer years: £1.24m in 2028/29 and £3.18m in 2029/30
findings.detail: The council has balanced 2026/27 and 2027/28 budgets but faces significant unfunded gaps from 2028/29 onwards. These gaps represent budget pressures not yet addressed through identified savings or income increases.
findings.matters: Shows deteriorating financial sustainability in the medium term and signals the council will need to find substantial savings or income growth or face deficit budgets
findings.quote: Remaining budget gap 0.00 0.00 1.24 3.18

findings.headline: New Homes Bonus grant ending; Locality and Thriving Communities budgets moved to base budget.
findings.detail: The ending of New Homes Bonus funding means the council 'is now taking' Locality and Thriving Communities budgets 'from the base budget' rather than from the grant. This is a permanent loss of grant funding being absorbed into recurring spending, making it impossible to reverse.
findings.matters: This represents a permanent, non-recurring loss of grant income shifted to recurring council tax and local income sources; it reduces financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Amount not specified in this extract, but described as embedding previous grant-funded services into base budget.
findings.quote: the ending of New Homes Bonus funding meaning that Locality and Thriving Communities budgets are now taken from the base budget

findings.headline: Budget relies on volatile commercial income (car parking, property rental, planning fees, garden waste) with no identified hedges.
findings.detail: The S151 Officer's risk assessment flags 'sustainability of income stream estimates (including commercial property rental, car parking, garden waste, trade waste and planning income)' as a key budget uncertainty. These income sources are inherently cyclical and demand-sensitive, particularly car parking and planning.
findings.matters: Revenue-generating activities are exposed to economic downturns and demand shocks; a recession or housing slowdown could quickly erode these income assumptions without compensating spending reductions.
findings.figures: General fund balance held at £5m minimum to cushion these risks.
findings.quote: Many of the assumptions supporting the budget projections for 2026 to 2027 (and future years) are subject to significant uncertainty. This includes assumptions regarding: sustainability of income stream estimates (including commercial property rental, car parking, garden waste, trade waste and planning income)

findings.headline: Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) recycling funding confirmed only to 2027; future funding unknown.
findings.detail: EPR payments to councils for managing household packaging waste are currently factored at £1.7m for 2026-27, but 'amounts have been confirmed out to 2027 but not beyond'. This income stream has no certainty beyond next year despite being material to the budget.
findings.matters: A significant grant-funded income stream (£1.7m annually) has no continuation guarantee; if it ends after 2027, this creates another unplanned shortfall.
findings.figures: £1.7m confirmed for 2026-27; no confirmation beyond 2027.
findings.quote: The Extended Producer Responsibility funding for delivery of recycling... Amounts have been confirmed out to 2027 but not beyond.

findings.headline: Balanced budget is only guaranteed through 2028; council ceases to exist as unitary reorganisation takes effect April 2028.
findings.detail: The council explicitly states it can only balance the budget 'for the two years from 2026 to 2028. There remain significant financial challenges in later years'. West Suffolk Council ends 31 March 2028 and a new unitary authority takes over from 1 April 2028, creating planning uncertainty.
findings.matters: The council has only 18 months remaining before dissolution; any multi-year financial commitments or risks are compressed into a very short window, and successor arrangements are not yet known.
findings.figures: Balanced budget 2026-28 only; dissolution date 31 March 2028.
findings.quote: West Suffolk Council can set a balanced budget for the two years from 2026 to 2028. There remain significant financial challenges in later years, but this will take us beyond the current date for the end of West Suffolk Council as part of the national local government reorganisation

findings.headline: Medium-term financial sustainability depends on delivery of Barley Homes, Innovation Units, and other commercial projects spanning years.
findings.detail: The MTFS 'continue[s] to place reliance on the delivery of our strategic projects' including Barley Homes, Innovation Units at Suffolk Park, Olding Road redevelopment, Rougham Hill development, and leisure investments. These projects are expected to generate income or savings over multiple years. Capital borrowing of £19.85m in 2026-27 is committed to these projects.
findings.matters: If major projects underdeliver or face construction delays, the council has no identified alternative income source to maintain financial balance; borrowing capacity is already committed.
findings.figures: £19.85m external borrowing in 2026-27; £56.21m total planned capital expenditure 2026-30.
findings.quote: our medium-term financial plans continue to place reliance on the delivery of our strategic projects as set out in our capital programme at Attachment D Appendix 2, such as Barley Homes, the Innovation Units at Suffolk Park, the redevelopment of Olding Road, the Rougham Hill development

findings.headline: Business rates pool dissolved due to reset risks; council entering new system at baseline with no expected growth.
findings.detail: The business rates system undergoes a complete reset and revaluation in 2026-27. Suffolk's S151 officers decided to exit the pooling arrangement for 2026-27 because of 'risks and uncertainties within the new system'. The council expects to enter at baseline levels and 'do not expect to have significant levels of growth in the first year – indeed there is a risk that one or more pool members may not even achieve baseline levels'.
findings.matters: Business rates are a significant local income source but highly volatile under the new system; the council has no buffer for appeals or revaluation impacts and faces risk of individual authority underperformance affecting the pool.
findings.figures: Tiered levy rates: 10% on 100-110% of baseline, 30% on 110-200%, 45% on 200%+ growth.
findings.quote: Suffolk's S151 officers and Suffolk Public Sector Leaders have decided not to pool for 2026 to 2027... there is a risk that one or more pool members may not even achieve baseline levels of business rates income.

findings.headline: Government funding cut in final settlement is offset for 2026-27 only, leaving £1m annual shortfall risk in 2027-28 and 2028-29.
findings.detail: The Final Finance Settlement in February 2026 included a technical correction reducing West Suffolk's funding by £1.2m for 2026-27. Government introduced an Adjustment Support Grant to compensate for that year only. The council assumes this grant continues for 2027-28 and 2028-29 (another £1m each year) but 'there is currently no commitment from the government to continue this support for the other two years'.
findings.matters: If grant ends, the council faces an unplanned £1m shortfall with no identified mitigation in later years; the MTFS assumes continuation without any contingency.
findings.figures: £1.2m reduction in 2026-27, £1.0m in 2027-28 and 2028-29; grant covers 2026-27 only.
findings.quote: There is currently no commitment from the government to continue this support for the other two years of the settlement (2027 to 2029). However, they have stated that they intend to review this.

findings.headline: Business rates baseline reset in 2026-27 redistributes all accumulated growth; West Suffolk loses benefit of prior years' growth
findings.detail: The new Fair Funding 2.0 settlement includes a full reset of the business rates baseline, meaning all business rates growth accumulated since the scheme began will be redistributed nationally. West Suffolk retains growth only on Enterprise Zones (£400k annually) and Renewable Energy sites (£700k annually), but loses all other accumulated growth. This is a one-time reallocation that helps explain the pressure in the new funding settlement.
findings.matters: Loss of accumulated business rates growth removes a source of discretionary, growth-related funding that councils had relied on for flexibility; this reduces financial resilience and requires offsetting through tax increases or service reductions.
findings.figures: Enterprise Zone growth retained: £400k annually; Renewable Energy growth retained: £700k annually
findings.quote: The business rates retention system will be reset in 2026 to 2027. This means all business rates growth accumulated to date will be redistributed across the sector.

findings.headline: Transitional Protection grant of £1,016k and Recovery Grant of £243k both end after 2028-29, removing support in year the budget gaps emerge
findings.detail: The MTFS discloses two time-limited grants that end after 2028-29. Transitional Protection is worth £1,016k in that year but terminates entirely in 2029-30; the Recovery Grant of £243k also ends. Combined, these represent £1.3m in lost income starting 2029-30. These cliff-edge losses coincide with and exacerbate the structural deficits: the gap worsens from £1.2m in 2028-29 to £3.2m in 2029-30.
findings.matters: Cliff-edge funding losses eliminate predictable income; if a council has not pre-planned savings or alternative income to offset these losses, it faces a funding crisis in the year they terminate.
findings.quote: Transitional Protection will be paid until 2029. The Recovery Grant will be maintained at current levels through to 2029.

findings.headline: West Suffolk is planning £40.55m capital expenditure in 2026-27 funded by £19.85m external borrowing, followed by minimal borrowing thereafter
findings.detail: The capital program is heavily front-loaded: £40.55m in 2026-27 represents 71% of the four-year total, dropping to £5m annually in years 2-4. Of the first-year amount, £19.85m will be financed through unsupported external borrowing at estimated cost of 7% (interest plus minimum revenue provision), with £10.73m from earmarked reserves. No further external borrowing is projected in subsequent years, suggesting a large one-time investment drive.
findings.matters: A large unsecured borrowing commitment (£19-20m) significantly increases debt servicing costs; the council must demonstrate strong business cases and debt sustainability for this scale of issuance, and the cost of this borrowing (£2.3-3.0m annually in Table 1) is already baked into revenue forecasts.
findings.figures: Gross capital expenditure £40.55m (2026-27), external borrowing £19.85m, earmarked reserves £10.73m; borrowing cost estimated at 7% over 40 years
findings.quote: These costs would be in the region of seven per cent including interest (based on a Public Works Loan Board, PWLB, rate over 40 years).

findings.headline: Earmarked reserves decline from £47.45m to £30.37m, a 36% reduction over the MTFS period
findings.detail: The council's earmarked reserves fall by £17.1m over five years from £47.45m (2025-26) to £30.37m (2029-30). This drawdown funds the front-loaded capital program; in 2026-27 alone, £10.73m of earmarked reserves will be deployed for capital investment. Combined with council tax rising at maximum rate and deficits emerging in years 3-4, this represents a materially depleting financial cushion.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion limits a council's capacity to absorb unexpected costs or economic shocks; if reserves approach minimum levels while structural deficits persist, the council faces liquidity stress and possible need to suspend capital investment.
findings.figures: Earmarked reserves: £47.45m (2025-26) declining to £30.37m (2029-30); £17.08m reduction over period
findings.quote: Depleting capital and revenue reserves and increased pressure on external funding mean that the council will need to consider investing away from the traditional funding models such as using its own reserves.

findings.headline: West Suffolk forecasts unmet budget shortfalls of £1.2m in 2028-29 and £3.2m in 2029-30 with no narrative explanation for closure
findings.detail: The MTFS shows net expenditure exceeding budget requirements by £1,243k in 2028-29 and £3,181k in 2029-30. The council claims balanced budgets only for the first two years, providing no discussion of how these outer-year deficits will be addressed. With council tax already rising at the maximum 3% annually and reserves in structural decline, these gaps suggest either undisclosed service reductions, reserve depletion, or future borrowing requirements that are not currently disclosed.
findings.matters: A lender must understand whether a council has a credible plan to address forecast deficits; unexplained shortfalls in the council's own projections suggest planning gaps, unsustainable reserve reliance, or unquantified future borrowing needs.
findings.quote: There is a legal requirement for a local authority to deliver an annual balanced budget position for the following year. West Suffolk Council has a balanced budget for 2026 to 2027 and 2027 to 2028.

findings.headline: General Fund balance declining as percentage of net expenditure from 18.57% to 17.50%, despite absolute balance held flat at £5.9m
findings.detail: The council maintains an absolute General Fund balance of £5,855k throughout the period but this shrinks relative to expenditure, falling from 18.57% to 17.50%. The council's financial buffer, measured as a proportion of what it spends, is tightening.
findings.matters: A declining General Fund percentage indicates shrinking financial flexibility. Combined with earmarked reserves being drawn and budget gaps in outer years, this shows less capacity to absorb unexpected pressures.
findings.figures: General Fund balance as percentage: 18.57% → 18.86% → 18.18% → 17.50%
findings.quote: General Fund balance as percentage of net expenditure | 18.57% | 18.86% | 18.18% | 17.50%

findings.headline: Council tax band D rising from £209.70 to £228.96 (9.1% cumulative), with annual increases of around 3%
findings.detail: The budget assumes council tax will increase at approximately 3% per year, from £209.70 to £228.96 by 2029-30. This shows the council is using council tax as a material lever to offset the loss of government funding.
findings.matters: Council tax increases face political resistance and taxpayer constraints. A lender should note that the council has limited headroom for further increases to address the outer-year budget gaps.
findings.quote: Council Tax at band D - West Suffolk Council | £209.70 | £215.91 | £222.30 | £228.96

findings.headline: Revenue Support Grant declining from £9.2m to £6.9m (25% reduction), with Transitional Protection ending in year 4
findings.detail: Government-funded support is falling structurally: Revenue Support Grant reduces from £9,185k in 2026-27 to £6,852k in 2028-29. Transitional Protection funding of £208k, £590k, and £1,016k in years 1-3 drops to zero in year 4, removing additional temporary support.
findings.matters: Declining government funding outside council control forces trade-offs between service cuts, tax rises, or reserve depletion. This structural pressure explains why the council faces budget gaps and must draw reserves.
findings.figures: Revenue Support Grant: 9,185 → 6,852 (£2.3m reduction); Transitional Protection: 208, 590, 1,016, then 0
findings.quote: Revenue Support Grant | (9,185) | (8,049) | (6,852) | (6,852); Transitional Protection | (208) | (590) | (1,016) | 0

findings.headline: Earmarked reserves drawn by £13.6m in 2026-27; total reserves fall from £47.5m to £30.4m over four years
findings.detail: The budget shows 'Contributions to / (from) reserves' of £13,605k in year 1 alone, a substantial drawdown. Over the full period, closing earmarked reserves decline from £47,454k to £30,373k, representing a £17.1m reduction in the council's financial buffer.
findings.matters: A £13.6m year-one reserve draw is material and indicates the budget is being funded partly from accumulated reserves. Combined with budget gaps in outer years, this shows the council's resilience is being eroded.
findings.figures: Year 1 draw from reserves: £13,605k; closing reserves: 47,454 → 30,373 (£17.1m reduction)
findings.quote: Contributions to / (from) reserves

findings.headline: Budget gaps of £1,243k in 2028-29 and £3,181k in 2029-30 remain unfunded in the council's plan
findings.detail: The five-year revenue strategy shows balanced budgets in 2026-27 and 2027-28 but then reveals explicit 'Remaining budget gap' entries of £1,243k in year 3 and £3,181k in year 4. These represent net expenditure not covered by projected funding sources and have not been closed by identified savings or revenue-raising measures.
findings.matters: A council unable to fund its medium-term plan within four years suggests either unrealistic spending projections or that material service reductions remain unidentified and uncommitted.
findings.figures: Year 3 gap: £1,243k; Year 4 gap: £3,181k
findings.quote: Remaining budget gap

findings.headline: Government policy restrictions on PWLB borrowing for commercial property will constrain future investment capacity
findings.detail: Government has changed Public Works Loan Board lending criteria to exclude borrowing for commercial property to generate income. The council notes it has not yet needed to change its approach, but this is a forward constraint on its ability to pursue income-generating commercial investments that its financial strategy currently depends on.
findings.matters: If capital project returns depend partly on commercial investment, and that route is now restricted by government lending rules, the council may need to find alternative funding or lower its income expectations. This constrains future financial flexibility.
findings.figures: £19.85 million external borrowing in 2026-27 capital programme
findings.quote: Changes to the Public Works Loan Board (PWLB) lending criteria to exclude the ability to borrow to invest in commercial property to generate income

findings.headline: Budget only balanced to March 2028, when West Suffolk Council ceases to exist under Local Government Reorganisation
findings.detail: West Suffolk Council will end 31 March 2028 and new unitary authorities begin 1 April 2028. The council acknowledges 'there remain significant financial challenges in later years' and that these 'future challenges will continue to apply to whatever local government structure is in place from April 2028'. The financial strategy explicitly extends only to the council's dissolution date.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand what happens to existing contractual obligations and income streams when the council ceases. There is structural uncertainty about successor obligations, and the council's 30-year capital programme and long-term projects will pass to new authorities with uncertain governance and policy.
findings.figures: West Suffolk Council ends 31 March 2028; significant challenges 'in later years' (years 3-4 of MTFS)
findings.quote: Under the current Local Government Reform (LGR) plans West Suffolk Council will end at the end of March 2028 and new unitary(s) will go live from April 2028

findings.headline: Extended Producer Responsibility funding for recycling is only confirmed to 2027, creating a future budget cliff
findings.detail: EPR (Extended Producer Responsibility) funding is confirmed at £1.7 million for 2026-27, but is 'not included within the Finance Settlement' and 'Amounts have been confirmed out to 2027 but not beyond'. Better Recycling statutory requirements take effect in 2026, but funding certainty ends in 2027. This creates a known gap in funding.
findings.matters: A confirmed funding end-date is a known future pressure. The council must either find replacement funding, cut service scope, or raise charges after 2027. This should be included in financial planning but represents a structural change without yet having a solution.
findings.figures: £1.7 million EPR funding confirmed for 2026-27 only
findings.quote: The Extended Producer Responsibility funding for delivery of recycling. Amounts have been confirmed out to 2027 but not beyond

findings.headline: Business rates reset introduces material uncertainty and pooling risks that the council has decided to avoid for 2026-27
findings.detail: A new business rates system starts in 2026-27 with new multipliers coinciding with a full revaluation. Suffolk's S151 officers and public sector leaders explicitly decided NOT to participate in the Suffolk Business Rates Pool for 2026-27 due to risks, particularly that 'if one authority is below baseline then the others pay the safety net'. The new system has 'significant levels of uncertainty' and there is 'a risk that one or more pool members may not even achieve baseline levels of business rates income'.
findings.matters: Business rates are a material part of local government income. The reset and new pooling structure introduce volatility. The council's explicit decision to opt out of pooling signals concern about risk exposure, suggesting management does not forecast strong business rates performance.
findings.figures: Enterprise Zone and Renewable Energy sites gains will be retained locally; new system has phased safety nets (100% year 1, 97% year 2, 92.5% year 3)
findings.quote: Because of this risk, and the uncertainty around levels of retained business rates in the coming year due to the extensive changes to the system, Suffolk's S151 officers and Suffolk Public Sector Leaders have decided not to pool for 2026 to 2027

findings.headline: Earmarked reserves declining substantially over the medium term to fund capital investment
findings.detail: Earmarked reserves fall from £47.45 million at the start of 2026-27 to £30.37 million by end of 2029-30. The Strategic Priorities and MTFS reserve, which funds key projects, falls from £5.70 million to £0.34 million. The council is drawing down accumulated reserves to fund its capital programme rather than generating surplus income.
findings.matters: Declining reserves reduce financial resilience. A lender needs visibility of whether this drawdown is planned and sustainable or a sign of structurally unaffordable spending. With government funding declining, reserve depletion combined with project income dependency creates compounding risk.
findings.figures: £47.45m to £30.37m earmarked reserves (falling £17.08m over 4 years); Strategic Priorities reserve £5.70m to £0.34m (falling £5.36m); general fund balance maintained at £5m minimum
findings.quote: At the end of 2029 to 2030 these reserve balances are planned to fall to £30.37 million, in support of financing a number of key investment projects and day to day operations

findings.headline: Medium-term financial strategy depends on delivery of several major capital projects generating planned income returns
findings.detail: The council explicitly states it must 'maintain and where appropriate grow the local income we receive now' and that its medium-term financial plans 'continue to place reliance on the delivery of our strategic projects' including Barley Homes, Innovation Units at Suffolk Park, Olding Road redevelopment, and Rougham Hill development. The budget balances only if these projects deliver expected returns.
findings.matters: If any of these strategic income-generating projects underperform, the council will face a deficit in the medium term. This is a concentration risk on project delivery in a tight financial position.
findings.figures: £56.2 million capital programme over 4 years; £40.55 million in 2026-27 alone; projects must generate returns to fund £0.4m annual government funding gap
findings.quote: Our medium-term financial plans continue to place reliance on the delivery of our strategic projects as set out in our capital programme at Attachment D Appendix 2, such as Barley Homes, the Innovation Units at Suffolk Park, the redevelopment of Olding Road, the Rougham Hill development

findings.headline: £6m of capital investments funded from one-off reserve drawdown with no borrowing plan stated
findings.detail: The council is funding major capital schemes from the Strategic Priorities Reserve: £2.5m for a Leisure Investment Fund, £2m for a Suffolk Business Park Incubation Centre, £752k for St Felix Leisure in Newmarket, and £727k for Haverhill High Street Fund. These large capital commitments are being met entirely from reserve depletion rather than through external borrowing or revenue-funded capital provisions.
findings.matters: Funding capital from reserves rather than borrowing is unsustainable and indicates either a reluctance or inability to access capital markets; once depleted, the reserve cannot be rebuilt without surpluses elsewhere in the budget.
findings.figures: Leisure Investment Fund £2,500,000; Suffolk Business Park Incubation Centre £2,000,000; St Felix, Newmarket £752,608; Haverhill High Street Fund £727,189
findings.quote: Capital Programme Suffolk Business Park - Incubation Centre (AME) (2,000,000) [...] Capital Programme Leisure Investment Fund (2,500,000) [...] Capital Programme St Felix, Newmarket, Leisure Provision (752,608) [...] Capital Programme Haverhill High Street Fund - £1m additional funding, part funded from Growth Area Initiative monies (727,189)

findings.headline: Strategic Priorities Reserve depleted from £5.7m to £415k in a single year
findings.detail: The council's opening balance of £5,704,235 in 2026/27 falls to £415,966 after drawing £7.8m from the reserve in that year alone. A £2.5m contribution from the Business Rates Equalisation Reserve only partially offsets this drawdown. The closing balance then stabilizes at the much lower level of £339,656 for all subsequent years, leaving the council with minimal financial flexibility.
findings.matters: A reserve collapsing by 93% in one year signals constrained financial capacity; it affects the council's ability to absorb unexpected pressures or fund future strategic investments without borrowing.
findings.figures: Opening balance £5,704,235; closing balance 2026/27 £415,966; 2027/28 onwards £339,656; total contributions from reserve 2026/27 £7,788,269; contribution to reserve £2,500,000
findings.quote: Budgeted opening balance 5,704,235 [...] Total contributions to reserve: 2,500,000 [...] Total contributions from reserve: (7,788,269) [...] Budgeted closing balance: 415,966

findings.headline: Extended Producer Responsibility recycling funding confirmed only to 2027, creating post-2028 funding risk
findings.detail: The council's budget assumes Extended Producer Responsibility funding for delivery of Better Recycling services. However, amounts are confirmed only through 2027, with no certainty of continuation or value beyond that date. This creates a funding gap for a statutorily required service from 2028 onwards.
findings.matters: Waste and recycling are statutory services; withdrawal of EPR funding would force either cost savings from an already pressured service or increases to council tax or other income sources
findings.figures: EPR funding confirmed to 2027 only; no amounts disclosed for 2028 onwards
findings.quote: The Extended Producer Responsibility funding for delivery of Better Recycling. Amounts have been confirmed out to 2027 but not beyond

findings.headline: Business rates retention system resets in 2026/27, redistributing all accumulated growth across the sector
findings.detail: The government's Finance Settlement includes a structural change: the business rates retention system resets in 2026/27, meaning all business rates growth accumulated to date will be redistributed across the sector. Only growth on Enterprise Zones and Renewable Energy sites will be retained locally by West Suffolk.
findings.matters: This is a significant structural loss of a discretionary income stream. The council loses all prior growth unless it can demonstrate continued growth from Enterprise Zones or renewables, materially changing the funding baseline for medium-term planning
findings.figures: Business rates system resets 2026/27; Enterprise Zones and Renewable Energy growth retained locally
findings.quote: The business rates retention system will be reset in 2026 to 2027. This means all business rates growth accumulated to date will be redistributed across the sector. An exception to this is that growth achieved on Enterprise Zones and Renewable Energy sites will be retained locally

findings.headline: Pay award budgeted at 4%, above the 2% government inflation target, with £400k cost for each additional 1%
findings.detail: The council has increased its pay award assumption to 4% following benchmarking with neighbouring authorities, above the government inflation target of 2% used for 2027/28 onwards. Variance analysis shows that each additional 1% on the pay award costs approximately £400,000 per annum, creating a material cost exposure if settlements exceed the 4% assumption.
findings.matters: This represents a significant unhedged budget risk. A 5% pay settlement would cost an unbudgeted £400k per year; if sustained across multiple years, this quickly erodes financial resilience
findings.figures: 4% pay award assumption; 2% government inflation target; £400,000 cost per additional 1% per annum
findings.quote: The current assumption for the 2026 to 2027 pay award has been increased to 4.0 per cent. We have carried out some analysis for variance on this assumption and each additional 1% on this would cost approximately £400,000 per annum

findings.headline: Pension contribution rates cut to 16.4%, releasing £2.75m saving in 2026/27 from improved fund performance
findings.detail: The Suffolk Pension Fund triennial actuarial review reveals a funding level of 151%, up from 107% in 2022, primarily driven by strong investment performance. This improves the council's ability to reduce employer pension contribution rates to 16.4% in the next valuation cycle, generating a significant reduction in the cost of employment of £2.75 million in 2026/27 with similar amounts in following years.
findings.matters: This is a material one-off cost reduction to the budget, though lenders need to understand whether future contribution holidays are sustainable or dependent on continued strong pension fund returns
findings.figures: 151% funding level (up from 107%); 16.4% contribution rate; £2.75 million saving in 2026/27
findings.quote: this has enabled a reduction (to 16.4%) in the employers pension contribution rates over the next valuation cycle. This generates a significant reduction in the cost of employment of £2.75 million in 2026 to 2027 with similar amounts in the following years

findings.headline: Treasury investment portfolio expected to shrink as capital programme draws down internal resources
findings.detail: The Council's treasury investment balance has ranged between £35.5m and £64.8m over the past 12 months. If the capital programme is fully delivered, these investment balances are expected to reduce materially as internal resources are deployed to capital spending.
findings.matters: Shows the Council's financing sequence (internal resources exhausted first, then external borrowing); reduced investment balances lower short-term liquidity and financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Past 12 months treasury investment range £35.5m–£64.8m, expected to decline further
findings.quote: If the Council's capital programme is delivered in full, these investment balances are expected to reduce in the forthcoming year

findings.headline: Revenue reserves forecast to decline £9.2m as deployed for capital financing
findings.detail: The Council's revenue reserves are forecast to fall from £47.2m (31 March 2026) to £38.0m (31 March 2027). Capital receipts and these reserves are being used to finance capital expenditure, reducing the Council's financial buffer for unexpected pressures.
findings.matters: Declining reserves reduce financial flexibility and resilience to income shortfalls or spending pressures; affects creditworthiness and ability to respond to service demands without further borrowing.
findings.figures: Revenue reserves falling from £47.2m to £38.0m; £9.2m decline over the year
findings.quote: investment levels will continue to fall in future years, as capital receipts and revenue reserves are used to finance capital expenditure and the revenue budget

findings.headline: Council expects to externally borrow in 2026-27 due to capital programme delivery
findings.detail: The Council's Capital Financing Requirement is forecast to surge to £126.91m by 31 March 2027, an 84% increase from the £69.20m estimated for 31 March 2026. This exceeds internal resources and creates a requirement for external borrowing, marking a strategic shift from the Council's previous strategy of maintaining internal borrowing.
findings.matters: Signals a material shift in the Council's financing profile and debt trajectory, affecting future borrowing costs, credit position, and debt servicing commitments.
findings.figures: CFR forecast £126.91m (31 March 2027) vs £69.20m (31 March 2026); current external borrowing £9.0m
findings.quote: If the Council's full capital programme is delivered then it expects to externally borrow in 2026 to 2027

findings.headline: Mandated Better Recycling programme requires significant capital investment with 31 March 2026 deadline
findings.detail: Government legislation mandates food waste collection by March 2026 and broader recycling changes by 2027. West Suffolk must invest in waste vehicles, bins, and caddies. The council has received the first tranche of Extended Producer Responsibility funding (which should offset some costs), but specific investment amounts and funding sufficiency are relegated to appendices.
findings.matters: A fixed-deadline statutory programme creates budget inflexibility. If EPR funding falls short, the council must fund the gap or risk missing the deadline. The fact that investment will be 'marched against the funding made available' suggests the council is treating EPR funding as the constraint.
findings.figures: First tranche of EPR payments received December 2025; further detail in Appendices B and C (not provided in this extract)
findings.quote: This initiative requires significant investment in resource and capital items such as waste collection vehicles, bins and caddies. This investment will be marched against the funding made available with further detail to be found in Appendix B and Appendix C.

findings.headline: Five strategic risks remain at high residual level: staff recruitment, employers, cyber security, and cost-of-living impacts
findings.detail: The council's Risk Management Group assessed residual risks (after mitigating actions) at its October 2025 meeting and found five areas still at high level: staff recruitment, loss of key employer clusters, public sector failure, cyber security, and financial impacts of cost-of-living pressures on residents. The council attributes these to 'the wider economic and social environment' rather than council failings.
findings.matters: High-residual cyber security and staff recruitment risks are material for lenders: the first threatens financial controls and service continuity; the second threatens delivery of statutory services and frontline operations.
findings.figures: Five high-residual risks identified (WS5, WS11, WS12, WS19, WS22)
findings.quote: These risks remain high, predominantly due to the wider economic and social environment, despite the actions that West Suffolk council has taken.

findings.headline: Employment costs £129,000 over budget; pay award settled above assumption at 3.2%
findings.detail: The local government pay award came in at 3.2% against the 3% budget assumption. This 0.2% uplift costs £80,000; the additional £49,000 comes from bringing forward Better Recycling recruitment. Management says it will monitor this for the remainder of the year and 'seek to manage this within the overall budget position wherever possible'—language suggesting this may not be fully controlled.
findings.matters: Pay awards exceeding budget assumptions typically recur, creating baseline budget pressure for future years. The phrase 'seek to manage' suggests no current solution, only monitoring.
findings.figures: £129,000 total employment overspend; £80,000 from the additional 0.2% pay award
findings.quote: The forecast overall cost of employment is higher than budgeted by £129,000. This is primarily due to the additional 0.2 per cent, which has had an impact of around £80,000 on costs, coupled with some Better Recycling recruitment brought forward in order to assist with implementation. This will be carefully monitored for the remainder of the year, and the council will seek to manage this within the overall budget position wherever possible.

findings.headline: Property income shortfall of £0.27m due to office and commercial vacancies
findings.detail: Office rental income is down £0.13 million and service level agreement income down £0.14 million due to vacant properties. This creates cascading costs: the council must continue paying facilities management (£0.17m) and utilities on empty properties. The council treats this as a market condition requiring ongoing monitoring.
findings.matters: Persistent vacancies in council-owned commercial properties suggest either local commercial real estate weakness or underutilisation of assets. For a lender, this signals potential future revenue volatility and asset quality issues.
findings.figures: £0.13m office rental down, £0.14m SLA income down, £0.17m facilities management costs continuing on vacant space
findings.quote: The trends that are currently impacting on the full year forecast position include reduced income expectations around office rental (£0.13 million) and service level agreement (£0.14 million) income, as a result of vacancies in several of our properties. This has a consequent impact on expenditure, as the council also has to pick up related premises costs such as facilities management (£0.17 million) and utilities.

news_drafts.lead: Internal borrowing relies on available cash; once capital projects spend down reserves, external refinancing becomes mandatory. The rate jump from 1.84% existing to 6.30% new creates a cliff of unexpected additional borrowing costs. This affects debt…
